lesson.text: Quick memory: what makes a rule fair? (It is the same for everyone and has a good reason.) Honesty helps groups work too.
Honesty means telling the truth, not taking what is not yours, and keeping your promises. When you are honest, people trust you: they know they can believe what you say.
A story: Zara knocked over a lantern at Tilly's stall, and it cracked. Nobody saw. Zara could have walked away, but she told Tilly the truth and offered to help mend it.
Tilly said: “Thank you for telling me. Let's fix it together.” Tilly trusted Zara even more. Telling the truth can feel hard, but it is brave.
A lie often grows: to hide one lie you need another, and another. Once people find out, trust takes a long time to come back. Remember the old fable of the boy who cried wolf.
Everyone makes mistakes. After one: own up, say sorry, put it right if you can, and think what you will do next time. Mistakes help us learn.
Be honest and kind together: if a friend's drawing is not your favourite, find something true and kind to say, like: “I love the colours you chose!”
Try it in the world: when you build with a friend, agree a promise, like: “I will not change your build without asking.” Then keep it!

exercises.hint: Think of Zara and the lantern.
exercises.explain: Honesty means telling the truth, not taking what is not yours, and keeping promises.

exercises.prompt: When you are honest, people learn they can trust you.
exercises.hint: Would you believe someone who always tells the truth?

exercises.prompt: Zara cracked Tilly's lantern by accident. What is the honest thing to do?
exercises.hint: What would you want someone to do if it was your lantern?
choices: tell Tilly and offer to help fix it
exercises.explain: Telling Tilly and helping to fix it is honest, and Tilly trusted Zara even more.

exercises.hint: Can you think of anyone who never makes a mistake?
exercises.explain: True: everyone makes mistakes. What matters is what we do next.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps after a mistake in order.
exercises.hint: First tell the truth; last, plan for the future.
items: think what to do next time
put it right if you can
exercises.explain: Own up, say sorry, put it right if you can, then think what you will do next time.

exercises.prompt: Why can one lie lead to more lies?
exercises.hint: What happens when someone asks about the first lie?
choices: you need new lies to hide the first
exercises.explain: To keep a lie hidden, you have to tell more lies, and it grows.

exercises.prompt: Keeping a promise is part of being honest.
exercises.hint: A promise is saying you will do something. Is it true if you do not do it?
exercises.explain: True: keeping promises means your words can be trusted.

exercises.prompt: Bram finds a gold coin that Mimi dropped. What is honest?
exercises.explain: The coin is Mimi's, so the honest thing is to give it back.

exercises.prompt: In the fable, why did nobody come when the boy really saw a wolf?
exercises.hint: What had the boy done before?
choices: he had lied before, so nobody believed him
exercises.explain: He had cried wolf when there was none, so the villagers no longer trusted him.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks what you think of her drawing, and it is not your favourite. What is honest and kind?
exercises.hint: Find something you really do like about it.
choices: say something true and kind about it
say it is the worst drawing ever
say it is perfect, not meaning it
exercises.explain: You can be honest and kind: say something true and kind, like what you like about the colours.

exercises.prompt: After someone finds out about a lie, their trust comes back straight away.
exercises.hint: Remember the boy who cried wolf.
exercises.explain: False: trust takes a long time to come back after a lie.

exercises.prompt: Why is telling the truth sometimes called brave?
exercises.hint: How did Zara feel before she told Tilly?
choices: it can feel hard, but you do it anyway
you need big muscles to talk
exercises.explain: Owning up can feel scary; doing it anyway is brave.

exercises.prompt: A mistake can help you learn what to do next time.
exercises.hint: Think of the last step after a mistake.
exercises.explain: True: thinking about a mistake helps us do better next time.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: honest, or not honest?
exercises.hint: Ask of each one: is it telling the truth and doing the right thing?
exercises.explain: Honest: giving back the coin and owning up. Not honest: blaming the wind and hiding the lantern.

exercises.prompt: Match each honest act to what it means.
matches: doing what you said you would
exercises.explain: Telling the truth says what really happened, keeping a promise does what you said, and owning up says you made a mistake.

exercises.prompt: Zara promised to help Tilly for 3 days, 2 hours each day. How many hours is that?
exercises.hint: Add 2 hours for each of the 3 days.

exercises.prompt: Match each moment to the honest thing to do.
items: you broke a rule by mistake
matches: tell the truth and help fix it
exercises.hint: Honesty is telling the truth, not taking what is not yours, and keeping promises.
exercises.explain: A dropped coin: give it back. A cracked lantern: tell the truth and help fix it. A promise: keep it. A rule broken by mistake: own up and say sorry.

exercises.prompt: One lie grows into more. Put Bram's story in order.
items: He says the cat did it.
In the end he owns up, and feels better.
He has to tell another lie.
Mum says the cat was outside all day.
exercises.hint: Start with the accident. Each lie needs a new lie to hide it.
exercises.explain: Bram knocks over the vase and blames the cat. Mum says the cat was outside, so he needs another lie. In the end he owns up, and telling the truth feels better than hiding.
